sections.text: A Vec<T> is a list that can grow and shrink. It's the collection you'll use most often.
Read items by index, or more safely with get, which returns an Option in case the index is out of range:
Loop over a vector with for. Borrow it with & to read, or &mut to change items in place:
Iterators make common jobs short: v.iter().sum::<i32>(), v.iter().max(), v.iter().map(|x| x * 2).collect::<Vec<_>>(), v.iter().filter(|x| **x > 10).count().
for p in prices (without &) moves the vector into the loop, so you couldn't use prices afterwards. Borrowing with & keeps it.

hints: The vector needs two more items at its end. Which method adds one item at the end?

quiz.question: Which method adds an item to the end of a Vec?
quiz.explanation: Vec has push, which adds an item at the end. add and append_one don't exist (append is a real method, but it moves all items from another Vec).

quiz.question: What does v.get(99) return when v has 3 items?
quiz.explanation: get returns an Option: Some(&item) if the index exists and None if it doesn't, so a bad index never crashes. Writing v[99] instead would panic.

quiz.question: How do you change every item of v inside a for loop?
quiz.explanation: for x in &mut v gives a mutable reference to each item, so you can change it with *x. v.read() doesn't exist, and for mut x in &v only makes x itself mutable, while the items stay behind a shared reference.
